title: Design has outgrown the traditional designer
text:
Design has outgrown the traditional designer

Why design education must reconsider the kind of student it imagines.

For decades, design offered artistically inclined students an appealing compromise. They could pursue a practical career without giving up creativity. Someone with visual talent learned typography, composition, color, image-making, and a collection of professional tools. With enough skill, that student could turn artistic ability into commercial work without the uncertainty of pursuing a career as a traditional artist.

That understanding of the designer still influences recruitment and what many aspiring designers expect from the profession. Design is often presented as a field where creative people can produce visually compelling work while building a recognizable career. The appeal is understandable, and generations of exceptional designers entered the profession through exactly that route.

I know this because it’s how my journey began. I was good at drawing, interested in art, and attracted to a profession that offered a practical outlet for my creativity. That foundation served me well, but it would not have been enough for the career I eventually built.

As the profession changed, I learned to code, moved into user experience and interface design, honed my strategic and business thinking, and developed an interest in the ethical and theoretical questions raised by technology. My career evolved because I did not remain confined by the traditional designer persona.

After two decades in professional design and now as a design educator, I see a growing mismatch between that persona and the profession students are preparing to enter. Students who are comfortable producing visual work are not always interested in research, systems, ethics, technology, or the reasoning that precedes a design decision. Those subjects can feel secondary to the creative work they expected to do, even though designers are now routinely responsible for them.

Artistically inclined students still have a place in design, and replacing them with technically inclined students would solve nothing. What matters is whether students are curious about the questions that now surround the artifact, including how it functions, whose interests it serves, and what consequences it produces.

It is easy to blame AI for disrupting the traditional role of the designer, but the profession’s transformation began much earlier— AI has simply made it more visible. Designers increasingly work on digital products that require attention to behavior, navigation, accessibility, technical constraints, business goals, and decisions affecting entire systems. While traditional design has always involved solving problems, the scope of those problems and the designer’s responsibility for addressing them have expanded.

Labor data offers one practical indication of where the profession is moving. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment for graphic designers to decline 2 percent between 2025 and 2035, while employment for web and digital interface designers is projected to grow 6 percent. The agency also expects automated tools, including AI, to make graphic designers more productive and reduce the number of workers needed.

In 2025, the median annual wage for graphic designers was $62,960, compared with $104,000 for web and digital interface designers. Technology-sector salaries may account for part of the difference, but the market's direction is clear. Employers are paying more for designers who can work with digital products, technical systems, user behavior, and product strategy than for those whose expertise is primarily visual. Traditional visual skills still have value, but they no longer command the same demand or economic value on their own.

Hiring research reported by Figma reinforces this broader shift. While visual polish remained important to 58 percent of hiring managers, it was only one capability within a much wider profile. More than 45 percent also identified collaboration, systems thinking, and product strategy as critical, while 73 percent reported increasing demand for proficiency with AI tools and 79 percent for knowledge of AI product design. Employers are not abandoning visual craft. They are seeking designers whose visual ability is joined with technical, strategic, and systemic knowledge.

I see the mismatch most clearly when students reach the parts of a project that precede the visual work. They may be eager to design screens but impatient with research, resistant to technical constraints, or inclined to treat strategy as documentation to complete before the real design begins. Technology is sometimes learned well enough to operate but not well enough to question.

These reactions are not simply failures of effort. Many students entered the field expecting a professional outlet for artistic creativity. A discipline increasingly concerned with behavior, systems, evidence, and consequences can feel like a change in the terms of that promise.

Changing the curriculum without changing the recruitment pitch leaves that mismatch intact. Programs that present design primarily as a practical outlet for creativity will attract students who expect creative expression to organize the profession. Their frustration is understandable when the education they encounter reflects the realities of contemporary design rather than the false expectations that brought them to the field.

Design programs should therefore reconsider what they advertise and what they evaluate during admissions. A visual portfolio can remain part of the process without serving as the only meaningful evidence of potential. Applicants could also explain how they understood a problem, considered conflicting needs, or changed a decision after encountering new evidence. An imperfect artifact supported by thoughtful reasoning may reveal more than a polished portfolio organized around personal style.

Recruitment could also extend beyond students who already identify with art. Future designers may come through psychology, computer science, business, sociology, communication, or philosophy because they are interested in behavior, technology, organizations, culture, or ethics. Their entry would expand the design field's capabilities rather than displace its artistic students.

The same shift should appear in teaching and evaluation. Projects could require students to defend consequential decisions rather than merely present finished work. Critiques could examine how they responded to conflicting user, technical, and organizational needs. Capstone projects could include evidence of research, iteration, ethical reasoning, and collaboration alongside the final artifact. This would not diminish visual craft, but it would place craft within the broader judgment contemporary design requires.

The profession needs people who can understand consequences not visible in the final artifact. For example, decisions that make an interface simpler, faster, or more personalized may also transfer control from its user to the system behind it. Designers must understand whose interests those systems represent and what users give up for convenience. Such consequences cannot be judged by looking at the screen alone.

This type of responsibility also explains why design will survive AI—despite all the doom and gloom. Generative systems can produce graphics, layouts, interfaces, and variations with extraordinary speed, reducing the number of people needed for visual production. But producing possibilities is not the same as determining which are worth pursuing. Organizations will still need designers to define the purpose, decide whose needs take priority, evaluate consequences, and accept responsibility for the result.

In this new landscape, creativity also takes on a broader meaning. It can appear in framing a problem, exposing a hidden assumption, reorganizing a system, or deciding not to build a proposed product. A beautiful design artifact may demonstrate exceptional craft while serving a system that should never have existed.

Designers whose primary value comes from operating tools and producing polished artifacts will increasingly compete with systems capable of doing that work. Those who can interpret complex situations, make defensible decisions, work across disciplines, and direct those systems toward worthwhile purposes occupy a less replaceable position.

The future of design education depends on more than revised courses, certificates, and new software. Programs must reconsider the person they imagine when they describe a future designer. Artistic imagination remains valuable, but it must be joined by curiosity about research, technology, systems, and the consequences of design decisions.

title: You can’t grow roses in a cornfield
text:
You can’t grow roses in a cornfield

A conversation with Whitney Hess, on careers, whispers, and where to plant yourself

Some questions sound administrative but are not, and “why do you want to switch jobs?” turns out to be one of them. I asked it on a mentoring call in the way you would ask about notice periods or portfolio order, one practical item among several, and the designer on my screen began to cry. Neither of us expected it. We sat with it for a moment, the way you do when a video call suddenly contains something real, and when she tried to answer, the answer had very little to do with jobs.

I brought this moment to Whitney Hess, who spent a decade as one of the most visible independent UX consultants of that era, based in New York for much of it with clients around the world, before consciously shifting her business from consulting to coaching, and who has therefore listened to more designers talk about their careers than almost anyone alive. She was not surprised. Long before people can say out loud that the work no longer fits, she told me, they hear it as a whisper: a quiet, dismissible sense that this is not what they want. The whisper is patient. Left unanswered it does not fade but grows, until one day it has become a daily shout, and a person finds herself crying on an ordinary mentoring call without quite knowing how she got there.

I have been interviewing designers who left the craft, or reshaped it into something new, for a book I am slowly writing about what is happening to our profession. Whitney is firmly in the second camp, and she will correct you if you suggest otherwise: she has never left UX, and she keeps her identity as a UX designer today. What she changed was the shape of the work, and she changed it while everything was still going up: the clients were blue-chip, the blog was widely read, the field itself was ascendant. That is what makes her worth listening to now. Most of us only examine what we really want when circumstances force the question, and she examined it voluntarily, at the height of a thriving practice, while the whisper was still at whisper volume. Since it is the quiet season, and half the industry is out of office with more time to think than usual, her story seems worth telling at length.

What the whisper actually says

Whitney’s move out of consulting was not a leap, and it did not begin with dissatisfaction. She registered her company in 2005, went fully independent about three years later, and built the kind of practice most designers would consider a destination: Scientific American, WNYC, the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. The trouble, when it arrived, arrived inside the work rather than around it. “I wasn’t really addressing the systemic problems” she told me. A project would end, the deliverable would be good, and the organization that received it would remain exactly the organization it had been before. So she began pulling her clients’ own teams deeper into the work, partly for better outcomes and partly because, as she put it, it “felt weird not leaving the company in a better place.”

It is worth noticing what the whisper was actually saying, because it was not saying quit; it was saying something more precise. It was telling her which part of the work was hers: less the solving than the facilitating, less the deliverable than the people gathered around it. The signs were public long before she acted on them. In 2012 she wrote on her blog that her consulting role had become “kind of like that of a group-therapist,” which reads today like a diagnosis published in plain sight; within eight months of writing it she had enrolled in a yearlong coaching training. The certification did not change what she was. It caught up with what she had already become.

The biggest challenge is how you design your career.

The economics of listening

The economics deserve to be told plainly, because this is the part that career-change stories usually leave out, and because Whitney, it turns out, has crossed twice.

The first crossing was the raw one. In 2008, after three years of running her consulting business on the side, she left her full-time job to make it her whole livelihood, and the numbers underneath that decision were thin: about three months of savings, in New York, with no institutional net. “It was terrifying,” she told me, and she meant it concretely enough that she had decided she would work at Starbucks if that was what staying independent required. What she had instead of a cushion was a track record of a particular kind. “I’ve always trusted my ability to figure it out,” she said. “I knew I was going to be resourceful.” Designers will recognize that sentence, because it describes the psychological posture of every project we have ever started: a new domain, unclear requirements, stakeholders we have never met, and a working assumption that within a few weeks we will understand the problem better than the people who handed it to us. It is a strange kind of confidence, empirical rather than temperamental, assembled from having been dropped into the unknown many times and having found the shape of it each time. Whitney’s real innovation was pointing that confidence at her own livelihood.

The second crossing, into coaching in 2013 and 2014, looked nothing like the first, and the difference is the lesson. By then she had significantly more savings, and she kept taking UX consulting projects while the coaching practice ramped up, winding one income down as the other grew. The first crossing she survived on nerve; the second she designed. In time the coaching revenue found its footing, and the consulting decade turned out not to be a sunk cost at all. Those years were what allowed her to sit credibly across from the senior leaders she now coaches, which is to say the practice she wound down kept working for her inside the practice she built.

The people who arrive

It would be easy to file what Whitney does now under career services, and the label would miss most of it. People rarely bring a career to a coach because everything is fine, and the field she serves keeps producing a particular kind of trouble. It is full of accidental leaders, she observes: craft people promoted into managing others because that was the only ladder on offer, now spending their days in meetings, mourning the work their hands used to do. Designers at large, she has noticed, see themselves as problem solvers and business growers and are received as people who make nice things, and they extend endless empathy to their users and almost none to their own kind, or to themselves. “We take a lot of responsibility on our shoulders,” she said of her profession.

So the coaching rarely stays inside the career, because the career is rarely where the trouble actually lives. Her question for clients is not what the next role should be but something quieter and harder: what is their best self, and what would work look like if it were built around it? It is the same instinct that surfaced in her consulting days, the group-therapist tendency she once joked about on her blog, matured into the job itself. It also explains her list of interests better than any career-services framing could. A coach who follows her clients’ troubles all the way down will end up talking about money, about grief, about what remains when the title is gone, which is to say she ends up coaching a life, and the career only as the part of it that happens between nine and five.

In defence of detours

The part of our conversation I have thought about most came when I asked what is next for her. Instead of an answer about deepening the coaching practice, she gave me a list: she is interested in financial advising, in training as an end-of-life doula, and, she added with a smile, in private investigation.

The list sounds eccentric until you trace where each item comes from. The interest in finance grew out of twenty years of running her own business, and out of the money questions her clients keep carrying into sessions, since you cannot coach someone about their career for very long without talking about what the career is for. The doula interest grew out of grief. She lost a few people close to her in recent years, accompanying those endings at close range, and emerged knowing something she could offer other people in the hardest passage of their lives. Even the private investigator idea, the one that made us both laugh, is her day job wearing a trench coat: she is paid to read systems, incentives, and decision makers, and to notice what everyone in the room is leaving unsaid.

None of these are exits, in other words. They are continuations, experiences she already owns waiting for a context that wants them. Underneath them sits a view of careers that is quietly radical: a working life is not a ladder within one profession but a body of accumulated experience that can be recombined, more than once, into new work. “The decisions that we make now become the legacy that we leave,” she said at one point, and the word legacy is doing real work in that sentence. She thinks about careers on the scale of a whole life, endings included, which may be why becoming a doula does not strike her as a change of subject.

Held up to that light, your own history gets interesting quickly. The banking designer who has spent five years inside compliance reviews is, whether she thinks of it this way or not, becoming an expert in regulated systems. The design lead who has survived three reorganizations has learned things about organizations that consultants charge for. We rarely see this in ourselves, because we are looking at our job titles, and a job title is a summary written by someone else, for a purpose that was never ours.

Where you plant yourself

None of this means growth is purely a matter of will, and the sentence that gave this piece its title was about the limits of it. “You can’t grow roses in a cornfield” Whitney said. Your ability to grow depends to an uncomfortable degree on the environment you are planted in. A cornfield is not hostile; it is optimized for corn. An organization that understands design as decoration will not, through any effort of yours, come to understand it as systems thinking, and the career path available to you inside any company is a function of how mature its design practice is, rather than of what your ambition deserves. Careers, in her telling, transfer no better than components do. “You cannot design one widget and expect it to work in every app in the app store,” she said.

The biggest decision they need to make is where they plant themselves.

Her practical advice follows from the metaphor. “The biggest decision they need to make is where they plant themselves,” she said of the designers she coaches, and she talks about that decision the way people talk about buying property: “I wouldn’t buy a house without doing my research on the neighborhood.” Designers, meanwhile, routinely join companies knowing less about the design culture than they would insist on knowing about a place they were going to live. Who does design report to? What happened to the last three senior designers? Does the career ladder exist anywhere outside the recruiting deck, and has anyone actually climbed it? These are questions you can ask in an interview, and asking them tells the company something about you that works in your favor.

Speaking as someone who runs a design team inside a large bank, I can confirm the information is not hidden. People will tell you how design really lives in their organization, sometimes proudly, sometimes bitterly, usually within ten minutes. We run more discovery for a two-week feature than most of us run for a five-year employment decision, and there is no good reason for that asymmetry.

Running discovery on yourself

What I take from Whitney’s story, and what I would like to hand to the designer from my mentoring call and to everyone quietly carrying some version of her whisper, is not reassurance. The market is hard at the entry level, unstable in the middle, and strange at the top, and reassurance would be a kind of lie. What her story offers instead is a method, and it is one designers already practice daily on other people’s problems.

It begins with discovery, pointed inward. The research question is not which job titles you could plausibly get. It is which moments of the past five years felt like yours, and what people keep bringing to you that appears nowhere in your job description. Whitney’s whisper named the facilitator inside the problem solver. Yours is likely to be similarly specific, if you give it the kind of patient attention you would give a user interview.

It continues with an inventory. Somewhere in your history is experience that feels off-topic: the failed side business, the caregiving years, the community you moderate, the domain you absorbed by accident. On the ladder model of a career this is clutter. On Whitney’s model it is material, and some of it is closer to becoming work than you think.

Then comes the audit of the soil, which is the uncomfortable step, because it can return the finding that nothing is wrong with you while something is wrong with the field you are planted in. The move that follows is not necessarily out of design. Sometimes it is only out of the cornfield.

And then you prototype, cheaply and early, the way she did both times. The consulting business ran for three years on the side before she trusted it with her livelihood, and the coaching practice ramped up while consulting still paid the bills. The jumps were real, but each was the last step of a long prototype rather than the first step of a plan. Mentoring one person, taking one course, writing one essay: these are the paper prototypes of a next career, and they cost about as much as paper.

What holds it together is the kickoff feeling, that trained confidence in your own resourcefulness. It is not Whitney’s private gift. It belongs to the profession, built into all of us by every project that started in fog and ended in shipping. UX has always attracted people who want their work to mean something, and that appetite survives any particular job, which is exactly why it aches when the job stops feeding it.

A question for a slow afternoon

Near the end of our call Whitney said she wants to keep developing her skills “over the arc of my career,” and it was clear she meant the arc of a working life, forty-some years across however many professions those years turn out to contain. She likes variety, she told me: “I like having every day feel different.” “Life happens,” she reminded me. “All your life plans go out the window. Covid happens.” What survives is the why underneath, the boundaries you will not trade away, and a flexibility about nearly everything else, so that when an opening appears you are able to recognize it and move.

We need to be connected with our WHY.

I think about my mentee often. The tears were not a breakdown, as far as I can tell. They were information arriving, a whisper that had been ignored long enough to find another channel, and the kindest thing that moment did was make the question impossible to postpone any further.

So, in the spirit of the season, and with whatever slow afternoon you can find: what do you actually love doing? Not what you are good at, which is a different list, and not what pays, which is a third. If you trusted yourself the way you trust yourself at every kickoff, what would you scope first? Somewhere inside the job you have is the work you want, and finding it is not a leap of faith. It is a design problem, and you have been training for it your whole career.

Whitney Hess coaches creative leaders at whitneyhess.com. Her 2012 essay “Designing the Company, Not the Product” is where this story quietly begins.

This conversation is part of a series of interviews with designers who left the craft or reshaped it into something new, for a book in progress.

If the soil audit above left you wondering where you actually stand, I built a tool for that step: a free, scenario based self assessment, about ten minutes, and the output is a profile, not a grade. Treat it as a private room. You can take it at designlevel.io/assessment

And if you think I am wrong about any of this, tell me. The strongest corrections to my thinking have come from readers.

title: A Week In Atlanta, GA On A $36,000 Salary
text:
A Week In Atlanta, GA On A $36,000 Salary

Welcome to Money Diaries where we are tackling the ever-present taboo that is money. We’re asking real people how they spend their hard-earned money during a seven-day period — and we’re tracking every last dollar.

This week: a former product manager, who is an aspiring product marketing manager working in tech, and who makes $36,000 per year, spends some of it on career coaching session.

If you’d like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we’re not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.

Editor’s Note: This is a 2026 follow-up diary, you can read the previous diary here.

Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We’d love to hear your thoughts here.

Occupation: Former product manager (aspiring product marketing manager)
Industry: Tech
Age: 25
Location: Atlanta, GA
Salary: $36,000
Joint Income/Financial Setup:
Assets:
401(k): $69,000
HYSA: $12,500
Money Market Fund: $17,497
Roth IRA: $38,942
Debt: $3,042 (this is tentative due to an unemployment mishap)
Paycheck Amount: $2,892.89 (This fluctuates since I work two jobs, both with varying hours)
Pronouns: She/her/hers

Monthly Expenses

Housing Costs: $0 (I currently live with my family)
Loan Payments: $0
Spotify: $12
NYT Subscription: $6
Gym Membership: $29.99
Google One: $19.99
GRE prep resource: $9.99
Therapy: $60
Claude Pro: $20
Tithe: ~$200
Car Insurance: $0 (I paid this off in full at the start of the year)
Netflix: $0 (I’m on my family’s plan)
Debt: $2,994 (credit cards)

Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?
Yes — growing up in an immigrant household with a family of educated professionals, higher education was a requirement, and post-grad is the expectation. Luckily, my four-year university was covered by a state scholarship and my parents paid for the remainder and housing.

Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?
My parents generally talked about living below one’s means and saving aggressively. However, they didn’t really talk about investing. My brother educated me on starting an investment account when I was in college, which I’m very grateful for. 

What was your first job and why did you get it?
I was an ice cream server at age 16 because I wanted to buy my own clothes and fund weekend outings with friends.

Did you worry about money growing up?
No, I grew up in an affluent household and it was a privilege to not worry about money.

Do you worry about money now?
Yes and no. Yes — because I’m unemployed for the first time in my adult life for a long stretch of time (it’s been seven months now) due to an unexpected termination. While I saved somewhat aggressively when I was employed, I’m no longer able to save and invest at the same pace, meaning I feel very behind when it comes to my personal financial goals. However, I moved back home once I lost my job, so I no longer have to worry about rent and groceries, for the most part. This was the biggest blessing I could’ve imagined as I was considering signing a lease shortly before the termination occurred. 

At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?
I would say age 23 — but I’m 25 and I rely on my parents as a financial safety net now. I’m forever grateful for them.

Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
Nope.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day One: Monday

6:30 a.m. — I have a final interview today — a surprise in-person round that I’d been anticipating pretty much all of last week. I pray in bed before groggily getting up to throw on some workout clothes and dash to the gym.

7:00 a.m. — It’s glute day. I feel like giving up halfway through — oh, man — but I don’t. My body will thank me later (I hope). 

9:00 a.m. — I log into my first job (it’s a temporary role that’s mostly remote) and make a cal block for a three-hour ‘appointment’. I answer a few calls and eat breakfast: coffee, overnight oats with my homemade Greek yogurt (a life-changing staple, if you ask me). I make a cup of coffee before putting on some business casual clothes (for the first time in forever!) Then I drive to the interview.

12:00 p.m. — Interview complete and I’m relieved. The conversation with the hiring manager was nice, but I couldn’t fight the feeling that this job feels like a bit of a demotion compared to the scale and scope of work I did at my previous company. I think the hiring manager picked up on this because they curiously asked me if I hated it, I think in some attempt to understand why I ‘left’. So, I guess, the ‘org change’ answer wasn’t enough. Anywho, I try to remind myself that I want to make a career pivot, so this next step may not be as glamorous, but it will be an opportunity for me. I sure hope the price is right, though! The salary is still an enigma, but I won’t worry about negotiations unless there’s even an offer on the table.  

1:15 p.m. — I’m back home and back to work. I answer calls I missed and do some paperwork. I then make some smoked salmon on toasted ciabatta with cottage cheese and a bit of kimchi (weird combo, but tasty). I switch between a meeting with a developer for my second job and a coffee chat with a girl who works in the department of the second company I’m interviewing with. Funnily enough, right after the interview, I find out I’ve made it to the third round — eek! However, the call left me with reservations on the scope and power of my work at the other company too (sigh). 

4:15 p.m. — I finish out the ‘work’ day with a coaching call (ironically, I coach for my past role and help people get into the company that let me go). It’s a prescreen and the candidate wanted to book for a future session. 

6:45 p.m. — I have a bit of time before my scheduled social event of the day: a meet-up with college friends since one is in town for the week. I meal prep banana muffins for the gym and a bulgogi-flavored ground turkey and Korean sweet potato salad. It only takes like 35 mins total to make! I finish meal prep right before GRE class [Graduate Record Examination]. My plan, before my life blew up, was to go back to school next year. Nonetheless, I’m committed to knocking out my testing this year for good. Since I double-booked myself today, I listen to the class like a podcast as I hit the road. 

10:00 p.m. — Had a splendid time catching up with friends, and it makes me feel more like myself. Chatting about my life, or the mess that it feels like it is currently, with people who don’t shame or judge me, is so completely freeing. I eat my meal prep and snack on some carrots I’d brought from home.

10:30 p.m. — I’m back home, so I make some hot cocoa (this is part of my daily routine), chew some nuts, and resume interview prep. I have a very important interview coming up this week, so I have to create multiple ‘stories’ and memorize them each night. It’s annoying but I’m determined to make this work pay off.

12:00 a.m. — I snack on popcorn as I prep. Finally, I get an email confirmation for said ‘important interview, ‘ and it’s sooner than I expected — eek! I’m going to have to move around my work schedule to accommodate it (and possibly my sleep). 

Daily Total: $0

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Two: Tuesday

6:30 a.m. — Today is usually spin day at the gym BUT because I have a big interview tomorrow and I have to go to an event tonight, so I’m devoting all the time that I have to preparation. I skip class, catch a few more Zzzs, get up to pray, and then start cranking out my story examples for the interview. I take a break to apply to more jobs and get started on work emails from my first job. I finally take a break from multi-tasking between story prep, job hunting, and emails to shower.

8:45 a.m. — I have a couple mins before my long team meeting starts, so I make the quickest meal known to man: smoked salmon on toasted ciabatta with mashed avocado and cottage cheese. I sprinkle nutritional yeast flakes and sriracha on top, and toss it in the air fryer for a few minutes.

10:30 a.m. — I finish up a coffee chat and end up getting a referral for a role so I quickly finish that application. I plan on front-loading today’s tasks, so I can spend the rest of my hours job hunting and prepping for tomorrow’s interview. All the while, I try to fight my own intrusive thoughts since it will be seven months of unemployment for me tomorrow. Wowzers.

1:00 p.m. — I’m on an application rampage. I reach out to three friends for referrals and get responses pretty quickly — people are so nice. I intermittently check work emails and request payment from job number two (since that’s overdue). I will restart interview prep tomorrow.  

2:00 p.m. — Food break — it’s the same Korean bulgogi-inspired salad with some carrots. I do interview prep with Claude so it can take on an interviewer’s persona and I can get feedback. I actually end up running out of credits and purchase extra tokens *wow*. Like most people, I have a moral dilemma when it comes to AI, especially due to my current situation, but what can I say? It’s cheaper than a career coach (which TBH I might need). $20

5:00 p.m. — I have a session with my therapist, which allows me to vent about my frustrations and confusion with the current state of my life. She’s very helpful in reframing my outlook on life and the pressures I impose on myself out of anger. I’m definitely going to work on being less self-focused and instead, pour my time into meaningfully contributing to others. I made a note to sign up for a volunteer opportunity I’ve been eyeing but de-prioritizing due to job hunting.

6:30 p.m. — I have an event to go to, specifically to support a friend’s performance. I somehow managed to eat my meal-prepped dinner in the car: tofu stir-fry with black rice and beans with a fried egg. The event is fun, insightful, and a good opportunity to step out of my head and hang out with old friends. I leave feeling a bit lighter.

10:45 p.m. — I get home and have a catch-up session with my mom after not seeing her for two days. It turns into a post-therapy vent about how I’m feeling, and she does a great job of encouraging me through some tough love. I make some low-sugar hot cocoa and a cup of yogurt with peanut butter and a sprinkle of nuts. It’s time to resume interview prepping.

12:30 a.m. — Halfway through prep, I realize I’m actually still hungry, so I make cheese on toast and power through another Claude session. I’m tired but also feel hopeful and remind myself that my future will be bright. Positive reinforcement, babes! I hit the hay around 1:45 after a 20-minute scroll on TikTok.

Daily Total: $20

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Three: Wednesday

7:00 a.m. — Rise and shine! I slept in a lil’ bit today due to last night’s late-night prep session. I’m meant to do another one this morning, but gym first.

7:30 p.m. — I hit arms and run into an old college friend — we’re both surprised to see each other since we live in the ‘burbs.

9:00 a.m. — Start part-time job number one quite promptly. Part-time job number two sends me incorrect payment info, in addition to some unrealistic project expectations, so I level-set and plan to work on what I can on Thursday.  

11:00 a.m. — I run a mock interview with a stranger through this coaching website for jobseekers. It’s my first experience, and I find it incredibly helpful, especially given my AI interview coach agent has been a little too sycophantic these days. It also helps to expose some blind spots before my hour-long interview later this afternoon. 

1:00 p.m. — I begrudgingly end up paying for another sesh with a career coach. I did a few last year when I was beginning my job pivot, but clearly, I think I need to readjust my approach with someone on a more consistent basis. For a 15 min consultation, I spend damn near $50! I feel robbed, but yet again, I’m willing to do whatever I have to do to secure a full-time offer (within reason). I eat the same bulgogi meal prep for lunch. $48.52

4:00 p.m. — My hour-long interview leaves me feeling exhausted. I also fear I didn’t use the best, applicable examples. Nonetheless, I’m grateful for the opportunity and optimistic for more to come (where I can hopefully leverage MORE diverse examples).

6:00 p.m. — I take a break from worrying about my job hunt to make homemade yogurt in the Instant Pot. I also snack on some carrots, pretzel sticks, and oatmeal with some peanut butter (random, but we’re an ingredients household). I start reviewing my last GRE class (the one that I passively listened to on my way to a friend outing). I don’t finish the video but tune into the latest class.

8:20 p.m. — Wow, I actually fell asleep during a bit of class today. It was on Zoom and my face wasn’t on camera, but my instructor yelled, “Stay strong!” I’ve signed up for another mock interview sesh at 9 p.m., but I’m so tired, so I nap after class instead and stay in bed for an hour. 

9:30 p.m. — The medley of snacks reduced my appetite for a proper dinner, so I eat a bit of leftover black rice with scrambled eggs and bits of smoked salmon. I add some kimchi and avocado for good measure. I’m so sleepy so I stay in bed and watch the latest episode of Euphoria. At this point, I’m watching to critique its current direction. This is the first time I’ve watched TV in a while; it feels nice to relax a bit. I do an abbreviated TikTok scroll before my eyes glaze over around 11.

Daily Total: $48.52

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Four: Thursday

5:00 a.m. — It’s spin class time! The music is so good today, and I smile the whole time. The energy of the class is just so high — it definitely helps to improve my mood. 

9:00 a.m. — Back online — I have to do some fieldwork for job number one today. I make a smoked salmon sandwich with avocado and cottage cheese spread on ciabatta. I also make some of my instant Colombian coffee; it’s so yummy.

11:00 a.m. — I have an onsite appointment with a client. It goes well and I snack on a mini popcorn bag on my way back home, where I’ll finish up my work.

1:00 p.m. — I’m home. I air fry my bulgogi salad and it tastes like an egg roll in a bowl, definitely bookmarking for next time! I do another mock interview, and it’s super helpful. I also finish up client calls and notes from job number one.

4:00 p.m. — I have a career coaching call and ponder setting up another session, given my desire to secure an offer from one of the companies I’m currently interviewing with. Also, I hear back from the big interview from yesterday, and I’ve moved on to a Power Day interview (think: five-plus hours of interviewing). 

5:00 p.m. — I need to catch up on GRE studying but I’m starting to feel super tired. I was supposed to go to a startup event in the city, but given I have a third-round interview tomorrow, I decide it would be best to nap and then schedule another mock interview later tonight.  

7:30 p.m. — Dang, I’m still tired and I sincerely don’t know why lol. Anywho, I eat some kimchi stir-fry and egg meal prep with black rice. I then feel super nauseous (I’m unsure why) but I keep a nausea band around so all good.

9:00 p.m. — I do a mock interview with a peer who’s been unemployed for a year. I pray my fate is not the same and that she finds success in her latest interview. I practice a few targeted questions for tomorrow’s interview and get on the phone with a friend to discuss the upcoming Power Day and how I can best prepare. (If you can’t tell, my whole day revolves around interview prep). 

11:45 p.m. — I stop prepping and watch a few YouTube videos while enjoying my homemade yogurt with some peanut butter and fruit. I also buy a party ticket for Saturday. I fall asleep pretty quickly after that (following a typical TikTok scroll). $11.99

Daily Total: $11.99

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Five: Friday

7:30 a.m. — I struggle to get up — it’s been a struggle the past week and I think it has something to do with my nighttime scrolling. I skip the gym today to prioritize prayer and then interview prep. I eat some coffee overnight oats with peanut butter for brekkie. 

10:00 a.m. — I have a coaching call for a separate program that I’m in, and I decide that, given the changes in my employment, I would likely defer my participation in the program. It’s a hard decision to make, and I genuinely feel tears stinging my eyes. (I’m very Type A so it pains me when life doesn’t go according to plan). But I’m practicing surrendering my plans and letting things be, with the knowledge that they will work out in the end as they should.

11:00 a.m. — Time for the interview. While I performed well, I was stumped and discouraged by the question of my employment gap and felt myself spiralling into anxiety about the quality of my response. I text a friend for some reassurance and try to calm myself down. Today, I receive two additional interview requests. Next week will be very busy, and I have to ensure the same mistakes do not repeat themselves.

12:00 p.m. — I’m moving my scheduled test exam to a later date. With interview prep, I’ve had no time to prepare the way I should be preparing. Like most things in America, there’s a fee associated. I also book an hour sesh with my job coach so double whammy on my CC. $212.52

2:30 p.m. — I have a meeting and eat lunch: ciabatta with scrambled eggs, cottage cheese and smoked salmon with avocado. My boss for job number two is going out of the country next week without providing the resources I needed to finish a project. I’m annoyed but going to use his absence to focus on interview prep. I’m seeing a movie with a friend tomorrow so I buy tickets online. $18.38

4:00 p.m. — I’m having a mini breakdown over my interview performance earlier today since I was really interested in the role I was applying for, but I know that my employment gap was the elephant in the room I didn’t directly address. I also haven’t heard back from my final round interview so that only amplifies my anxiety. I take a break from my mental anguish to pay an outstanding fine at my library. I also pick up gum and an e.l.f. brow gel on the way home. $14

7:00 p.m. — I play pickleball with a friend and go out to dinner. I end up covering their meal since they paid for the court reservation, which was way more expensive than I expected. I leave the outing not sure if this turned into a date or not. He starts asking if I’m currently dating, which I’d tried and failed to do, mainly because at times, I feel like I don’t have much to offer without the identity and security that comes with a FTJ (dumb, I know). He doesn’t seem to care, though, and the conversation becomes less serious — TBD where things go, I guess! $25

11:30 p.m. — I help my mom with her hair for an event tomorrow and make a Ninja CREAMi ice cream while I catch up on the latest episode of Euphoria.  

Daily Total: $269.90

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Six: Saturday

9:00 a.m. — I sleep in and take some time to pray about some important decisions I have to make. My legs are very sore from pickleball, which I later discover during my morning leg day workout. I think I’ve pulled something in my knee. I make an egg salad sandwich with carrots.

1:00 p.m. — I clean my room and then go to the movies with a friend. We see Obsession, and we’re both unsure if the movie was as good as the TikTok reviews said it was, but I did enjoy the underlying messaging. After leaving the theater, my car battery dies unexpectedly. Luckily, I get a jump-start by a kind stranger at my friend’s apartment complex. I snack on some mini popcorn bags on the ride home and stop by an auto shop to make sure my car is okay. 

5:00 p.m. — I work on a presentation for an upcoming trip (mission trip) that I’m going on in the summer. I also start interview prep for next week, but I fall asleep. After my nap, I make a bowl of leftover kabob chicken, rice, kimchi, and avocado.

9:00 p.m. — I’m going to the club with friends but stop by a kava shop first to get a drink since I want to try a non-alcoholic alternative. I get a drink to split with a friend. $7.13

12:00 a.m. — We get to the club and our $12 tickets are no longer valid, so now we have to buy $25 tickets to enter the event. Yeah, not happening. I’m able to make a new friend who ‘sponsors’ my ticket and he generously pays for my friends as well. We all dance the night away, and I get home at 5 a.m

Daily Total: $7.13

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Seven: Sunday

12:00 p.m. — I have a very late start to the day. Due to a rainy weekend forecast, a friend’s picnic event has been cancelled. In anticipation of better weather to come tomorrow, I decide to focus on interview prep and finishing some items on my to-do list. But first, I watch church service online. It was good, as usual, and so I give my weekly tithe. $50

2:30 p.m. — I make avocado toast with smoked salmon, kimchi, and a small purple potato, sprinkled with nutritional yeast. The perks of living at home and with an immigrant family is I don’t have to buy most of my groceries. I recognize this is a privilege that I’m extremely grateful for (job or no job). That being said, I still go to the store to buy things that my family wouldn’t normally eat or purchase — I buy a tub of cottage cheese, protein cereal, gum, a small container of Greek yogurt, which serves as a starter for my homemade batch, and extra firm tofu for meal prep. We’re an ingredients household so we always have rice and frozen vegetables on hand. $22

7:00 p.m. — I finish my presentation and start interview prep work, which is essentially building several different STAR [Situation, Task, Action, and Result] stories. I take a break to catch up with my long-distance bestie. Our chats always lift my spirits a lil’. I eat my tofu and kimchi stir-fry meal prep for dinner.

11:00 p.m. — I call it quits on interview prep — I still need to create four more detailed stories for an upcoming multi-hour interview. I start doing GRE homework but abruptly realize I need a refresher, as it’s been way too long since I visited the topic. I make my pre-Memorial Day calendar intending to finish my interview prep stories so I can get back into GRE prep, and then start working on job number two items. I finish my remaining homemade yogurt with peanut butter and protein cereal (it tastes like ice cream!)

12:10 a.m. — Bedtime! I needed to make a decision by the end of today, as well as a few financial choices, given there are a couple of trips that my friends want to go on. Since my unemployment journey began, I’ve been the bottleneck to group travel, but I’m trying to not let my current circumstance always dictate my response and be optimistic for the future, instead of anxious over it.

Daily Total: $72

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Breakdown

Conclusion:
I think that my discretionary spending was way higher than usual. I typically don’t plan for three ‘fun’ outings per week, but I had a friend visit town. I also wanted to take advantage of the Memorial Day holiday, hence the party tickets. Recording my spending has also made me hyper-aware of the investments (both financial and mental) that I put into the job hunt. Now, I don’t think I necessarily NEED a coach to achieve my goals, but I want to ensure I’m putting 100% of my efforts into this search given the state of the economy and my future ambitions of going to grad school. In the future, I hope that I can make fun purchases without the anxiety and regret that accompany frivolous spending.

Update:
Needless to say, my life STILL feels like a work in progress and damn is it EXHAUSTING. I’m actively interviewing for my (theoretical) dream role while working my current full-time job. I’m also exploring what it means to find fulfillment outside of my 9-5 through social impact and creative writing. Although I still complain a lot about feeling stagnant and frankly uncertain about where my life will go, I’m grateful and blessed to be where I’m today. The journey continues.

Final side note: A lesson that I’m still learning is the importance of decoupling my worth from a role. Regardless of their title, the odd jobs that I held throughout my unemployment season played a pivotal role in my personal and professional growth. A career shouldn’t be defined by what you bring into a 9-5; it’s what you pour into your community through your curiosity, intelligence, and wit.

title: The Best Perfumes Of 2026, According To Our Fragrance-Obsessed Editors
text:
The Best Perfumes Of 2026, According To Our Fragrance-Obsessed Editors

In a beauty editor’s world, being forced to declare a favorite beauty category is like choosing a favorite child — you simply can’t expect us to pick. But we make no apologies for admitting that fragrance holds a very special place in our lives (and our routines).

A compliment on your perfume can be incredibly affirming, but there’s something even more poignant about fragrance’s ability to transform how you feel when you wear it purely for yourself. For us, fragrance is a constant: at the office, at the gym (controversially), and, yes, even at home when no one else can smell you. With that in mind, we take our fragrance very seriously here at Refinery29. Over the past few years, we’ve made it our mission to sniff out, test, wear, and discuss the latest launches alongside the classics — so we can recommend the ones that are truly worth your time, money, and shelf space.

That’s why we wanted to give the very best of them their moment in the spotlight with our Fragrance Awards 2026. From niche, under-the-radar houses to the biggest names in perfume, these are the 29 scents we’ve spent the past few years smelling, spritzing, and talking about with our friends and colleagues.

Who knows? You might even discover your new signature.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Best New Fragrance: Byredo Future Memories Eau de Parfum, $235 for 50ml

“Mark my words: Future Memories is going to become the fragrance Byredo is best known for, even usurping cult classics like Bal D’Afrique and Gypsy Water. At first spritz, it’s a generous pour of vanilla-steeped whiskey, but the intoxicating boozy notes soon unfold into tobacco-like iris butter, cozy orange blossom, and salty, skin-like musk. If a 1920s speakeasy were a fragrance — all cigar smoke, strong cocktails, and perfumed lapels — it would be this, despite the “future” in its name. And the staying power! I sprayed it on a jacket over a month ago, and it’s still as hypnotic as it was on the first day.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Luxury Fragrance: Penhaligon’s Halfeti Eau de Parfum, $330 for 3.4 fl oz.

“I would say the enduring popularity of Halfeti needs to be studied, but the reason is obvious: Nothing smells as expensive and seductive on my skin as this does. Even ten years after its launch, I have a hard time comparing it to anything else. Warm, cozy saffron, cardamom, and nutmeg jump out at first, but over time, creamy sandalwood, cocooning amber, and comforting musks come into their own, making it nuzzly and inviting. I love wearing it on my neck and wrists, and whenever I pull someone in for a hug, they never fail to compliment me. In fact, anything from Penhaligon’s is the epitome of luxury to me, but Halfeti trumps them all.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Drugstore Fragrance: Le Monde Gourmand Tomate Bébé, $30 for 30ml

“Le Monde Gourmand is known for its vast array of affordable eaux de parfums, and this past spring it added Tomate Bébé to its roster. The fragrance, made in collaboration with iconic Los Angeles restaurant Jon & Vinny’s, is everything an aspiring tomato girl wants to smell like. As the name suggests, it’s a vegetable-forward blend of green pepper, tomato leaf, and fresh basil, but with citrusy lemon verbena, skin-like ambrox, and a whisper of dessert-like caramel. The result? A perfume that’s good enough to eat — almost.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Niche Fragrance: Ex Nihilo Demon Dancer, $180 for 50ml

“Ex Nihilo is one of those brands perfume enthusiasts talk about in hushed tones, as if keeping it to themselves will help them gatekeep it — it’s that good. I’ve tried pretty much every scent from the niche perfume house and found favorites in Blue Talisman and Fleur Narcotique (the latter said to be adored by Hailey Bieber), but I think the latest addition to the brand’s burgeoning fragrance dynasty blows them all out of the water. Tart rhubarb, zippy peppermint, and sharp, green blackcurrant give it such an intriguing edge that you can’t help but smell yourself — the notes practically dance off the skin — while vanilla-esque tonka and warm musks ground it, making it the perfect everyday scent.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Designer Fragrance: Miu Miu Miutine Eau de Parfum, $108 for 30ml

“Strawberry scents had a big year (see: The 7 Virtues Strawberry Jam and Phlur’s Strawberry Letter), but I’d argue that no fragrance has captured the fruity note quite like Miu Miu’s Miutine — the house’s first new scent in six years. With notes of juicy strawberry, heady gardenia, warm brown sugar, and cozy vanilla, it’s everything the Miu Miu woman is: playful, feminine, and a little offbeat in the best way. And can we have a moment for the bottle, please? Inspired by Miu Miu’s iconic matelassé leather goods, it’s every bit as chic as the juice inside.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Celebrity Fragrance: Billie Eilish Your Turn II Eau de Parfum, $70 for 30ml

“Billie Eilish: Grammy-winning recording artist, Gen Z style icon, and…the front-runner in the celebrity fragrance game. One of her more recent drops, Your Turn II, is a darker, woodier interpretation of the original fresh-fruity scent. (In a 2025 interview, the singer actually revealed that Your Turn II was an earlier fragrance sample she’d loved but hadn’t ever seen the light of day.) I personally love the blend of more feminine perfumery with accords more commonly used in colognes. Case in point: jammy fig and cassis clashing with zesty vetiver and resinous olibanum. (Not to mention, the lasting power of this rivals some of my most pricey perfumes.) Safe to say, with it emerging as a fan-favorite, she made the right call rescuing it from the vault.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Genderless Fragrance: Lore Somewhere but Nowhere Eau de Parfum, $92 for 50ml

“I rarely ambush my husband with fragrances, but I’ll never forget the first time I sampled Lore’s Somewhere but Nowhere — and immediately knew I had to smell it on him. It cites Americana as its north star, but to me, it smells like home (or your person — more or less the same thing, really.) Its heart of cedarwood mixed with creamy cardamom and black tea (and a barely-noticeable touch of whipped vanilla cream) makes this one that I love as much on him as I do on me. Which means one thing: We’re going to need a larger bottle.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Everyday Fragrance: Merit Retrospect L’Extrait, $92 for 30ml

“Merit had no business going this hard with its fragrance debut, but hey, we’re certainly not complaining. The inaugural scent, Retrospect, is exactly what you’d expect from the makeup brand that mastered minimalism: Effortless yet impactful, and with a certain mysterious quality. No one note really stands out; you just smell really good. However, we can reveal the notes in the warm, sheer scent: Bright notes of citrusy bergamot and fresh pear meet a floral bouquet of jasmine, rose, and violet. The secret sauce, in my opinion, is in the base of warm vanilla, skin-like musk, and leafy moss, giving it a familiar finish. And because it’s an extrait (a more concentrated form of fragrance), you can expect this one to last all day long wherever you apply it.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Long-Lasting Fragrance: Diptyque Orphéon Eau de Parfum, $260 for 2.5 fl oz.

“During a closet clear-out recently, I pulled out a coat I hadn’t worn in over a year, and the scent that greeted me was unmistakable: Diptyque Orphéon. It’s the perfect paradox. Juniper berries give it a strong gin-and-tonic edge — a tall glass tumbler loaded with ice — while cedarwood, jasmine, and tonka bean evoke a church foggy with incense. The dry down is so special: powdery and comforting, like a blush compact from the ’90s. It’s the one perfume all my beauty editor peers agree on, and the staying power is truly second to none.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Compliment-Earner: Glossier You Doux Eau de Parfum, $82 for 50ml

“Glossier You Doux has earned me so many compliments; it was a front-runner for my wedding-day scent. (I ended up wearing it at my rehearsal dinner.) It’s easily the most wearable, romantic take on a woody fragrance I’ve tried, and like all of the Glossier You scents, it has a musky ambrox base that truly works on everyone. Along with toasted palo santo, it features delicate violet, spicy frankincense, and smoky myrrh. The result is an effortlessly alluring scent with truly unparalleled mass appeal.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Travel Fragrance: Dior J’adior Solid Perfume L’Or de J’adore, $109

“We’ve all seen Charlize Theron exiting a pool of liquid gold (or more recently, Rihanna sauntering through Versailles), but Dior’s solid perfume iteration, L’Or de J’adore, somehow makes the iconic scent feel more luxe than ever. Housed in a tiny gold compact that’s basically begging to double as a bag charm, this travel-friendly solid makes it easier than ever to bring your scent on vacay — without fearing it being confiscated by airport security. With notes of heady jasmine, sweet rose, and elegant violet wrapped in a warm, nectar-like finish, I think it’s bold, iconic, and unforgettable.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Office-Friendly Fragrance: D.S. & Durga I Don’t Know What Eau de Parfum, $225 for 1.7 fl oz.

“There’s a fine line between wanting to smell good at work and causing perfume cloud-induced headaches from two cubicles away. Here’s where D.S. & Durga’s I Don’t Know What comes in. It’s subtle but noticeable, with a clean, woody, skin-like quality that somehow smells like you — only better. The formula is built around a mix of bright bergamot, iso e super (a synthetic fragrance molecule with moody, amber-like notes), herbaceous vetiver, and musky ambroxan, creating an airy, balanced scent that lingers all day long on skin and clothes without alerting Brenda from HR. In other words, it’s office-appropriate without being boring, and transitions seamlessly to after-hours.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Wedding Fragrance: Commodity Milk Orchid Expressive Eau de Parfum by @Perfumerism, $155 for 100ml

“Commodity’s Milk Orchid was one of the most anticipated perfume launches of 2025, but the formerly limited-edition fragrance recently became a permanent fixture in the brand’s collection. Content creator Emma, aka Perfumerism, collaborated with Commodity to create a gourmand floral that feels elevated yet universally appealing. Creamy notes of fig and coconut milk swirl with orchid to create the perfect light-yet-impactful scent for your big day. This is truly special-event and signature-scent worthy!” — Sophia Dennis, head of programming and brand strategy for Refinery29 & Beautycon

Best Date-Night Fragrance: NOYZ Only Human Eau de Parfum, $85 for 1.69 fl oz.

“Some fragrances can’t help but take center stage. By contrast, NOYZ Only Human is more about making people lean in closer in a “What perfume are you wearing?” kind of way. Which is exactly why it’s taking home our award for best date-night scent. Warm, woody, and subtly sweet, it blends creamy cardamom, comforting sandalwood, dessert-like vanilla, and sultry musk into a skin-like scent that feels intimate yet totally effortless. It’s the kind of fragrance that smells even better up close. Conveniently, right where you want it for date night.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer. 

Best Skin Scent: Cyklar Flora Veil Roll-On Perfume Oil, $24

“If you find traditional floral scents annoyingly loud, you have to try Cyklar’s Flora Veil. It bypasses the heady, garden-in-full-bloom intensity entirely, redefining what a floral profile can be. When I first took a whiff of it, I instantly thought it smelled like me fresh out of the shower, but even better. It earns top honors in the skin scent department because of how masterfully it wears throughout the day. It starts with a delicate (not overly fruity) whisper of crisp raspberry that has just enough brightness to intrigue you without feeling sweet, and it melts seamlessly into a grounding, velvety musk base. Rather than sitting heavily on top of your skin or taking over a room, the oil formula literally warms up with your natural body chemistry, creating your own little bubble of a delightful-smelling aura. What makes Flora Veil so addictive — and why I grab it the most — is the I’m-not-trying-too-hard confidence it gives.” — Alexis Bennett Parker, Refinery29 director of shopping partnerships 

Best Hair Fragrance: Initio Atomic Rose Hair Perfume, $105 for 50ml

“I first smelled this hair perfume on a friend as I leaned in for a hug, and I couldn’t stop thinking about it. I had to buy one for myself, and now I reach for it more than my eau de parfums. Most hair perfumes apply with a whisper and disappear in the breeze, but this clings to strands like an extrait. Lush Bulgarian rose and powdery Turkish rose are heady and mesmerizing, while zingy bergamot cuts through with a hit of freshness. But it’s the vanilla that really sticks around — you’ll find yourself wanting to smell your hair throughout the day. Perhaps an odd habit, but one I can’t kick when I wear this.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Body Mist: Being Frenshe Matcha Me Hair, Body, & Linen Mist, $16.99 for 5 fl oz.

“Body mists are having a major comeback, and when I got a sneak peek (whiff?) of Being Frenshe’s new Matcha Me scent in the Hamptons this summer, I knew I’d found a new favorite. (I’ve been keeping the lab sample in my purse for mid-day touch-ups, and am glad to no longer keep it a secret.) It’s fresh, soft, and uplifting — just like your favorite matcha latte. Alongside the namesake tea note, there’s a hint of soothing vanilla (a favorite of founder Ashley Tisdale French, who also includes it in Vanilla Cashmere) and a soft musk that gives it a cozy, clean quality without veering sugary. Even better, it’s formulated to softly scent everything from your skin and hair to your linens and room for the ultimate relaxing mood.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Scented Body Wash: LOoPHA Oud + Amber Hand + Body Wash, $24.50 for 400ml

“Life’s too short not to make every shower a great-smelling one. LOoPHA (aka The Ordinary’s sister body care brand) has arguably mastered the art of the body wash, elevating the humble shower gel with its liquid and powdered body cleansers, which come in three scents: Oud + Amber, Chalk, and my personal favorite, Broadleaf Forest. There’s not a bad one in the bunch, but I can’t get enough of how crisp and clean (not medicinal) Broadleaf Forest smells. It’s cozy, grounding, and makes every shower feel like a moment of calm.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Scented Body Moisturizer: Brunel Pearl Glow Body Oil, $53

“Capturing that signature, sun-kissed Jasmine Tookes glow has been pinned to the top of my beauty mood board for years. Actually achieving it? Pure chaos. Traditional body oils often turn into a slippery mess, ruining fine silk and making crisp white linen an absolute no-go. But Brunel’s Pearl Glow is the holy-grail pivot. Pearl Glow smells effortlessly high-end. It opens with a bright burst of crisp red apple and warm solar notes that instantly transport you to a golden-hour beach day. As it settles into skin, it unfolds into a lush heart of jasmine petals and creamy almond, before drying down to a grounding, velvety sandalwood base that gives it a bespoke luxury perfume feel. What makes it an absolute award winner, though, is how seamlessly it balances top-tier perfumery with real-life practicality. You get that enviable, lit-from-within sheen without feeling heavy or sticky. Best of all, its dry-touch finish absorbs quickly with zero transfer onto white clothing, meaning you can finally bathe your collarbones in supermodel radiance and walk out the door completely stain-free.” — Alexis Bennett Parker, Refinery29 director of shopping partnerships 

Future Classic Fragrance: Parfums de Marly Delina Exclusif, $265 for 1 fl oz.

“Some fragrances have their moment before fading away; others feel destined to have one for years to come. Parfums de Marly’s Delina Exclusif falls firmly into the latter camp, earning our Future Classic award for its unapologetically luxurious take on the iconic fruity-floral Delina. A richer, moodier sibling to the original scent, it layers juicy lychee and crisp pear with Turkish rose, spicy incense, warm vanilla, and woody oud for a multifaceted, versatile scent that’s sweet but not saccharine. It’s the kind of perfume that instantly feels iconic — and I, for one, wouldn’t be surprised if, years from now, we’re still talking about it.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer 

Best Alcohol-Free Fragrance: Maison Francis Kurkdjian Kurky Eau Parfumée, $195 for 2.4 fl oz.

“Maison Francis Kurkdjian is known for fragrances that smell expensive and sophisticated (hello, Baccarat Rouge 540), but the luxury perfumer is far from a one-trick pony; Kurky Eau Parfumée is a literal and metaphorical breath of fresh air, thanks to its bright, fruity profile. It opens with juicy raspberry and peach mixed with soft florals, light-as-air musk, and creamy sandalwood. And unlike the vast majority of my perfume collection, this formulation is alcohol-free. (“Eau parfumée” literally translates to “scented water.”) As such, it feels less drying on skin than a traditional alcohol-based fragrance, and I also love using it as a hair mist to add scent and a hint of shine. The result is playful yet elevated, proving that an alcohol-free fragrance can have just as much personality as a traditional eau de parfum.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Fall Fragrance: Phlur Vanilla Canyon Eau de Parfum, $99

“To me, most vanilla perfumes are usually way too sweet, aggressively artificial, or smell like a walking dessert table, which is an instant pass. But Phlur Vanilla Canyon completely flips the script, taking the usually cloying note to grown-and-sexy territory. If you’re already obsessed with Vanilla Skin, consider this its darker, cooler, big sister. It has a smoky vanilla DNA that doesn’t read as buttercream. Think smoldering amber and intoxicating depth that feels grounded. What elevates Vanilla Canyon to true award status is how easily it grabs attention without ever feeling overpowering or suffocating. It gives you that warm, sultry vibe that stays close to the skin, kind of like a plush cashmere sweater, making people instantly lean in to ask what you’re wearing. It takes a note we all thought we knew and reinvents it into a masterclass in modern, mysterious perfumery.” — Alexis Bennett Parker, Refinery29 director of shopping partnerships 

Best Fresh Fragrance: Frédéric Malle Par Acne Studios Eau de Parfum, $295 for 50ml

“Fresh perfumes have somewhat faded into the background, both literally and figuratively, as deeper, heavier gourmands have come to dominate the fragrance conversation — and they’re not exactly known for their staying power, either. But Frédéric Malle Par Acne Studios refuses to be overlooked. It opens with a slightly soapy, aldehydic laundry note, but as it dries down, the magic happens. One whiff and you’re whisked away somewhere that feels as pure and weightless as a fluffy cloud, while still being sharp, crisp, and refreshing.” — Sophia Dennis, head of programming and brand strategy for Refinery29 & Beautycon

Best Gourmand Fragrance: Brown Girl Jane Chalet, $102

“Gourmand fragrances are built around edible, dessert-like notes, and Brown Girl Jane’s Chalet is like stepping into a high-end patisserie in Paris. Think white chocolate truffle offset by slightly bitter dark cocoa, plus ripe, syrupy plum and a dash of vanilla essence for good measure. But I think that the effervescent champagne note cuts through all that richness, making it surprisingly wearable rather than tooth-achingly sweet. It’s one of my most complimented perfumes.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Woody Fragrance: Maya Njie Nordic Cedar, $156 for 50ml

“I first came across Maya Njie’s Nordic Cedar in 2018, and it has been a linchpin in my perfume rotation ever since. If you like Phlur’s Father Figure, you’ll absolutely adore this. Crisp, green cedar and grassy patchouli are warmed up with a dash of cardamom spice and amber, while musk helps it melt into the skin, becoming an extension of you — like the natural scent of freshly washed skin after a long bubble bath. The bottle may be simple, but the juice inside is anything but. It’s layered and intriguing, equal parts fresh and sexy.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Floral Fragrance: Gucci Flora Gorgeous Orchid, $188 for 3.3 fl oz.

“Gucci Flora Gorgeous Orchid was the first floral perfume that I, a longtime floral perfume hater, genuinely loved. And if you suspect that florals simply aren’t for you, allow me to introduce you to the exception. Gucci Flora Gorgeous Orchid takes the traditional, occasionally stuffy perfume category and gives it a modern, gourmand-leaning twist, blending pâtisserie-like vanilla with airy ozonic notes (synthetic accords designed to evoke the atmosphere after a rainstorm) and a subtle vanilla orchid accord. It’s proof that a floral fragrance doesn’t have to smell like a flower shop — and that even a floral perfume skeptic can find their match.” — Karina Hoshikawa, Refinery29 senior beauty writer

Best Green Fragrance: Prada Infusion de Rhubarbe Eau de Parfum, $190 for 3.4 fl oz.

“If you like nothing more than a stroll through the farmers’ market on the weekend, Infusion de Rhubarbe will be right up your alley. Think tangy, crunchy stalks of rhubarb — green leaves and all — freshly pulled from the ground, still earthy and warm. Zingy bergamot, verdant green mandarin, and bitter orange oil add to its bucolic quality, balancing the rose note so perfectly that even those who think they dislike floral scents (me!) will fall head over heels for this. I love the fresh, airy cloud that follows me when I spritz it through my hair.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Oud Fragrance: Kayali Oudgasm Milky Musk Oud Eau de Parfum, $140 for 50ml

“Kayali’s entire Oudgasm collection is a total compliment magnet, but if you ask me, the most special and memorable scent of them all is Milky Musk Oud. It’s like a second skin, or pulling on your favorite cashmere sweater after a long soak in the tub. It’s all down to earthy suede, indulgent whipped cream, soapy white musk, and creamy sandalwood, with strawberry and, of course, oud — a fragrant, honeyed tree resin — adding a peppy sweetness. Unlike other oud scents, oud is the supporting actor rather than the star of the show, but it still has plenty of depth without being overpowering. I can guarantee people will ask what you’re wearing.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director 

Best Fruity Fragrance: Ellis Brooklyn Plum Tonic Eau de Parfum, $115 for 50ml

“Forget banana, strawberry, or coconut for a hot minute. The fruity note I’m reaching for this fall is purple plum. There’s something rich and brooding about it in all its ripe, syrupy glory, making it feel like a grown-up alternative to the saccharine — and, to be honest, a little juvenile — fruity fragrances out there right now. Plum Tonic is the antidote. It’s still sprightly and energetic thanks to sweet mandarin, while cool, cucumber-like violet leaf, acidulous acai, and warm, enveloping amber crystals give it the rich, complex depth I look for in a fruity fragrance.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Refinery29 beauty director

title: “We Have Not Been Forgotten”: Meet The Palestinian Designer Behind Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress
text:
“We Have Not Been Forgotten”: Meet The Palestinian Designer Behind Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress

Olivia Rodrigo may only be 23, but the pop star knows exactly who she is. The young singer has been vocal about supporting women’s rights since she was a teenager, and recently held the inaugural Daisy Chain Fields music festival — inspired by Sarah McLachlan’s Lilith Fair — raising $20 million USD for women’s charities. During a press conference for the festival, where she announced an initial $10 USD million donation, Rodrigo made waves by stepping out in a Palestinian-designed dress by Nöl Collective. At a time when Palestine is suffering under Israeli occupation, wearing a garment made on the ground with symbols of freedom on it was a strong statement.

“It helped say, ‘We are still here; we have not been forgotten’,” designer and founder Yasmeen Mjalli tells Refinery29. “It meant the world to us.” Mjalli isn’t sure how Rodrigo or her team discovered their fashion brand, but says they were honoured to be chosen, and stayed in contact with her team throughout the process. While the singer’s team suggested some general ideas for the silhouette that aligned with her classic style and the colour pink, Nöl Collective were given more free rein than one might imagine. “We had a lot of creative freedom in the details, such as the shade of pink — a soft and dusty rose — the type of material we use[d], raw silk, [and] details like the flutter sleeves, frilled neckline, the embroidery motifs and the embroidery colours,” the designer explains. “It was so much fun to be given the creative freedom to bring something to life that honoured Olivia’s style while also reflecting our own identity.”

The symbols on the dress are also more than just decoration. While the garment is beautiful, Nöl Collective knows the power that Palestinian embroidery can hold; representing a political reality, the natural world, and our dreams. The design house chose specific motifs to tie into Rodrigo’s ethos and what she stands for. “The flowers spoke to the theme of the Daisy Chain Fields festival. Flowers are incredibly important in our world; they decorate the land after rains, [provide] beauty after a storm, [support] ecosystems, [feed] wildlife, and sometimes [contain] medicinal properties,” Mjalli says. “In this particular instance, the daisy chain symbolizes the power of a united world in the face of adversity.” The dusty rose dress also featured embroidered birds, a clear representation of freedom — not just for Palestinians, but for all those who need it around the world.

Nöl Collective’s garments are handmade in Jerusalem, Gaza, Ramallah, and Bethlehem, and the fashion brand places a strong emphasis on showcasing the entire process. Mjalli knows fashion is inherently political, regardless of where a garment is made. “70% of garment workers in the world are women; it’s a women’s rights issue,” she says. “[And] because fashion has unfathomably detrimental effects on the environment, it’s also an environmental issue.” Fast fashion has been widely criticized for human rights violations and environmental impact, but it’s so easy for consumers to compartmentalize or ignore these issues.

“When you show how the garment is made, you humanize the process and close the gap that separates the consumer from the creator. The hope is that people are more mindful when buying because they can see how much time, labor and love go into a garment,” the designer explains. “We hope that for every garment we put out in the world, you can picture the hands of the women who made them — the same hands which brush hair, pick fruit, and hold children and grandchildren.”

It’s impossible to talk about Nöl Collective without acknowledging the impact the Israeli occupation has had on them. For Mjalli, it’s incredibly hard to put into words how difficult the process of creating garments has been. Moving between cities and towns now takes much longer due to military checkpoints, shipping orders is challenging due to border closures, and customs can destroy shipments at their discretion.

The fashion house uses natural fibres that it is unable to source locally, so it relies on shipments from overseas. Last week, a large shipment of naturally dyed and hand-woven wools from Indian artisans was rejected. “[It was] destroyed last week, simply because of who we are. This was devastating, because our production had already been delayed for months, meaning the collection would be released much later than needed,” the founder says. “We still had to pay the cost of shipping and for the fabric itself because the artisans still need to be paid for their labor, and then we still needed to buy replacement fabric.” The fashion house ended up having to start a GoFundMe to cover the excess costs because fashion and art matter, and it’s a form of resistance to keep going.

Mjalli wants people to understand how vital it is to support Palestinian businesses, especially those on the ground. “We are creating under impossible circumstances,” she says. “Every day, a door slams shut in our face, and we keep searching until we find another door to keep going. So many talented artisans here don’t get a chance, so supporting artisanal work on the ground here can profoundly impact the community.”
